Where it began

Ross Taylor was born in Lower Hutt on 8 March 1984. His mother is Samoan, and alongside the game his father taught him he grew up playing kilikiti, the Samoan form of cricket. He went to Wairarapa College and Palmerston North Boys' High School, and for a while hockey had as much of his attention as cricket.

Cricket won. He captained New Zealand's under-19 side, played club cricket in England as a young man, and made his senior debut for Central Districts in January 2003. He also carries the hereditary Samoan title of leaupepe.

The player

His one-day debut came in March 2006, and he was only the second man of Samoan heritage to represent New Zealand. Tests followed, and he played 112 of them between 2007 and 2022, scoring 7,683 runs at 44.67 with 19 hundreds. His best was a superb 290 in Australia in 2015–16, the highest score by a New Zealander playing away from home.

In March 2010 he reached a Test hundred against Australia from just 81 balls, the fastest a New Zealander had managed. He later made hundreds in all three Tests of a series against the West Indies, including an unbeaten 217, and in February 2020 he became the first cricketer to play 100 matches in each of the three international formats.

What made him special

Taylor was a clean striker of the ball, at his most dangerous through the leg side. With Kane Williamson he formed one of New Zealand's most productive partnerships; in that Test in Australia the two added 265 together. He was just as good in one-day cricket, where his unbeaten 181 against England in 2018 won a chase of 336.

He also bowled the odd off-break. His 3 Test wickets cost only 16.00 each, a rate the regular bowlers might have envied, even if his captains rarely put it to the test. In the field he held 163 catches.

Away from the middle

He won the Sir Richard Hadlee Medal for his seasons in 2012–13 and 2013–14, and in 2022 he joined the New Zealand Order of Merit as a Companion, honoured for what he had given to cricket and to Pacific communities. When he won a match award in his first game as captain, he gave the prize money to the Lansdowne club in Masterton.

His last match for New Zealand, in April 2022, was his 450th international. Then, in 2025, he came out of retirement to play for Samoa, his mother's homeland, making his debut for them on 8 October.

And finally

On his birthday at the 2011 World Cup he made an unbeaten 131 against Pakistan, becoming only the fourth batsman to celebrate with a one-day hundred. Most of us settle for cake.
